summary: Children partition continuous shapes (circles, rectangles) into two and four EQUAL parts, name them halves and quarters, and describe the whole as 'two halves' or 'four quarters'. The core ideas are equality of parts (equal in size, not necessarily the same shape), the part-whole relationship (equal parts recompose the whole), and that a shape can be partitioned validly in more than one way as long as the parts are equal.
misconceptions: Accepting unequal parts as halves/quarters because the number of pieces is right
Thinking a shape can only be partitioned one 'correct' way (rejecting valid alternative cuts)
Confusing the number of CUTS with the number of PARTS
Not seeing the whole as composed of its equal parts (cannot say two halves/four quarters make the whole)

activities.title: Cut it, check it, rebuild it
steps: Take a paper circle and a paper rectangle and fold or draw a line to make two parts.
Overlay or rotate the two parts on top of each other to check they match exactly (equal).

On fresh copies of the same rectangle, make two halves a DIFFERENT way (e.g. vertically, then horizontally, then a single diagonal through opposite corners) and check equality again. For the diagonal, cut along it and turn one triangle half a turn to lay it on the other, because folding a non-square rectangle along its diagonal will not make the halves line up.
Now partition a circle and a rectangle into four equal parts (e.g. the rectangle as four equal strips or a 2x2 grid) and check all four match.
Slide or stick the parts back together to rebuild the whole, saying aloud 'two halves make the whole' and 'four quarters make the whole'.
Label each partition with 'halves' or 'quarters' and count the PARTS (regions), not the cuts.
activities.insight: Halves are two equal parts and quarters are four equal parts; the equal parts together rebuild the whole, and the same shape can be halved or quartered in more than one correct way provided the parts are equal in size.

activities.title: Halves, quarters, or neither?
steps: Sort a set of partitioned shapes into three groups: 'halves', 'quarters', and 'neither'.
Include a shape split into two UNEQUAL parts (right number of pieces, wrong equality) to place in 'neither'.
Include a non-standard but valid cut (e.g. a diagonally-halved rectangle or a circle halved by a slanted line through its centre) to place in 'halves'.
For each decision, explain how you know, e.g. 'the parts are equal' or 'the parts are not the same size'.
activities.insight: Deciding whether a partition shows halves or quarters depends on whether the parts are equal in size, not on the number of pieces or on a familiar orientation.

activities.title: Diagnostic: unequal pieces with the right count
steps: Look at a circle divided by an off-centre line into two clearly unequal parts, and a rectangle divided into four parts where three are small and one is large.
Answer: 'Is the circle cut into two halves? Is the rectangle cut into four quarters? How do you know?'
Then answer: 'If you put the parts of the rectangle back together, what do they make? Is there more than one way to cut the circle into two halves?'
activities.insight: Having the right NUMBER of pieces is not enough; halves and quarters must be EQUAL parts, which together recompose the whole, and there can be more than one valid partition.

checkQuestion: Show a circle divided by an off-centre line into two clearly unequal parts, and a rectangle divided into four parts where three are small and one is large. Ask: 'Is the circle cut into two halves? Is the rectangle cut into four quarters? How do you know?' Then ask: 'If you put the parts of the rectangle back together, what do they make - and is there more than one way to cut the circle into two halves?'
checkAnswer: No to both - the parts are not equal. Halves are two equal parts (a line through the middle); quarters are four equal parts. Put back together, the four equal quarters make the whole rectangle, and a circle can be halved by any line through its centre (more than one way).
